revisions.title: The invitation, with conditions
revisions.body: Socrates’ route from the Academy to the Lyceum is interrupted by Hippothales and Ctesippus at the gate by the spring of Panops. Their summons points him toward a newly built wrestling-school where the group spends its time chiefly in conversation. But entry is not automatic: Socrates asks both on what terms he may enter and who the beautiful one is. When Hippothales blushes at the question, Socrates declares that he is already far advanced in eros.

revisions.title: Proximity and concealment before the questions
revisions.body: The movement of bodies anticipates the argument: Lysis approaches after Menexenus has taken a seat, while Hippothales stays screened and listens. One way to read this staging is that friendship first appears as a problem of proximity and visibility. Socrates then turns the gathering toward comparative questions and the claim that friends share what they have.

revisions.title: Knowledge, not age, earns authority
revisions.body: Socrates shifts the measure of authority from age and rank to competence. Lysis says his parents permit what he knows; Socrates then widens that principle from household management to Athenian affairs and the Great King’s kitchen, where superior judgment would outrank both family and royal succession. The argument is conditional: one is entrusted when one appears wiser in a given domain.

revisions.title: A rehearsal before the real question
revisions.body: One way to hear this transition is as a small test of friendship itself. Lysis asks Socrates to carry the conversation into his friend’s presence, then wants to remain close when the exchange becomes adversarial. Socrates’s declaration that he values a friend above wealth therefore arrives not as detached doctrine, but as a desire enacted in the room.

revisions.title: Reciprocity tested by reversal
revisions.body: The reciprocity thesis is not the passage’s final landing. One-sided love first makes the mutual answer untenable; the proposed repair is that neither is a friend unless both love. Socrates then appears to reverse the candidate: the beloved seems to be the friend even while hating, but that makes friends into enemies, so the lover is restored. Read this as a recursive test, not a single march to aporia: after the reversals, Lysis doubts the inquiry itself.

revisions.title: Neither formula settles friendship
revisions.body: I read this exchange as a stress test for two attractive formulas. On that reading, “opposite befriends opposite” sounds explanatory until the conversation turns it against friendship with an enemy, then against justice and goodness. The passage need not announce a third category; its sharper achievement is to leave both formulas under pressure. What, then, might friendship require beyond resemblance or opposition?

revisions.title: A demanded endpoint, not yet a discovery
revisions.body: Here the regress yields a requirement, not a result. If each friend is friend for the sake of another, the argument must either continue indefinitely or arrive at a first friend; it then distinguishes that supposed endpoint from the instrumental friends pictured as its images. The passage does not establish that such a first friend exists or identify it.

revisions.title: A causal shift, not a final answer
revisions.body: The exchange first tests the claim that bad causes friendship: desires that are neither good nor bad would remain when bad things vanished, and desire would still involve love (claim_lysis_0023). It then offers desire as a new candidate cause (claim_lysis_0024; claim_lysis_0025), before naming oikeion as what love, friendship, and desire concern (claim_lysis_0026). Hear these as successive proposals, not one identity: the passage has not yet settled the account (claim_lysis_0024; claim_lysis_0025; claim_lysis_0026).

revisions.title: Aporia without a settled definition
revisions.body: Here the argument reaches an aporia, but not a proof that every account of friendship has failed. Socrates’ summary is conditional: if none of the loved, loving, like, unlike, good, akin, or other examined candidates is a friend, he has nothing further to say (claim_lysis_0030). The pressure is cumulative: the oikeion proposal revives rejected like-to-like consequences (claim_lysis_0027; claim_lysis_0028; rel_lysis_0001), while identifying good with oikeion yields only the conditional that good is friend to good (claim_lysis_0029; rel_lysis_0001). One way to hear the ending is as exhaustion of this inquiry, not a settled definition.
